name: Tamanu oil
lead: Tamanu oil is a viscous green-yellow oil pressed from the nuts of Calophyllum inophyllum, a coastal tropical tree of the Indo-Pacific. People use it on the skin in the hope of fading scars and dark marks, calming acne and giving skin a smoother, healthier look, drawing on a long tradition of use for wounds, burns and skin complaints in Polynesia, India and Southeast Asia [1][2].

In skin care it is sold as a pure oil and as an ingredient in creams and serums, listed on labels as Calophyllum inophyllum seed oil [2]. It is promoted for scars, blemishes, dryness and skin soothing, and marketing often cites its resinous fraction and compounds such as calophyllolide and 4-phenylcoumarins [1][2].

Laboratory work reports that a Polynesian tamanu oil emulsion stimulated proliferation and collagen production in cultured human skin cells [3], and rat studies have examined its effect on wound healing [7][8]. No completed human trial for scars or acne was found.

paras: The oil comes from the single large seed inside the round fruit of the tamanu tree. Fruiting happens twice a year, in May and November, and the kernel makes up about 43 to 52 percent of the dry fruit weight; fresh kernels are roughly 55 to 73 percent oil, and dried kernels about 70 to 75 percent [1]. Kernels are traditionally pressed in wooden or stone presses called ghani [1]. The tree grows to 20 to 30 metres, tolerates salt and wind, and is widely planted along coasts, with major oil production in Madagascar, Vietnam and French Polynesia [2].

Calophyllum inophyllum, known as tamanu, kamani, beautyleaf, oil-nut, mastwood and bintangur, is a large evergreen tree native to the Old World tropics from East Africa through South and Southeast Asia to Australia and Polynesia, including Hawaii. Austronesian migrations carried it to Oceania and Madagascar, and it is now cultivated widely in the tropics as an ornamental.[11]

In Polynesia, mastwood groves planted at marae, sacred sites, were regarded as the abodes of spirits, and the wood was carved into tiki and appears in chants and folklore. The tree's curved limbs formed the keels of Austronesian outrigger ships.[11]

The oil is bluish-yellow to dark green and viscous, with a resin fraction of 10 to 30 percent; main fatty acids are oleic, linoleic, stearic and palmitic, and it contains compounds such as calophyllolide and 4-phenylcoumarins.[1] Composition varies by geographic origin across the South Pacific.[4]

The oil has an unpleasant taste and smell from its resin, which refining can reduce [1]. Other components reported include friedelin and inophyllums B and P [1]. Calophyllolide, isolated in 1951, was the first neoflavone found in nature [1]. A study of oils from across the South Pacific found that levels of bioactive components relate to geographical origin [4].
Most commercial use is in skin care.[1] Grokipedia lists its INCI name and a comedogenic rating of 2 attributed to a safety source.[2]

Tamanu has been used in Polynesia, India and Southeast Asia for healing wounds, burns, eczema, acne and psoriasis [2]. In northwest Luzon in the Philippines the oil once fuelled night lamps, and in southern India it was used for waterproofing cloth, as a varnish and in soap [1]. Commercial use today is mostly skin care [1]. Its name varies by region, with Polynesian terms such as fetau and mu u [1].

Beyond skin care, the oil was a lamp fuel in northwest Luzon and, according to Wikipedia, was used to fuel radio generators in World War II. Fatty acid methyl esters from the oil are reported to meet US and EU biodiesel standards, though those yield figures are marked as needing citation.[11] Leaf and flower poultices appear in traditional medicine, and a cited study reported flower extracts active against pathogenic bacteria.[11]

In vitro, a Polynesian tamanu oil emulsion promoted keratinocyte and dermal fibroblast proliferation and glycosaminoglycan and collagen production, and showed wound-healing activity in cell tests, with gene-expression changes in treated cells [3]. Another study developed resinous ethanol-soluble extracts of French Polynesian tamanu seed oil to improve its antioxidant properties [9].

In rats, a study of 21 animals compared tamanu oil, Centella asiatica and saline on uniform skin wounds, with biopsies taken at 7, 14 and 21 days. Tamanu-treated wounds had less wound contraction, and on day 7 showed more macrophage-rich granulation tissue, fibrosis and collagen density, which the authors interpreted as accelerated tissue formation [7]. A 2024 study formulated tamanu oil bigels as an anti-scarring product, combining molecular docking with a full-thickness excision wound model [8].

A 2021 review discusses tamanu oil's potential in atopic dermatitis, based largely on in vitro and animal studies of anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antimicrobial and wound-healing properties [5]. Formulation papers use tamanu oil as a component of delivery systems, such as an emulgel carrying levocetirizine tested in a mouse atopic-dermatitis model and polymer wound dressings with silver nanoparticles [6][10].

Grokipedia reports low toxicity and no irritation at low concentrations and a comedogenic rating of 2.[2] Wikipedia does not discuss allergy.[1] Because it is a nut-derived oil, labels and dermatology references generally note the possibility of skin sensitivity; no controlled human safety study is available.

Separate from the pressed oil used in cosmetics, the Calophyllum inophyllum tree has toxic parts. The mature fruit is poisonous to humans and has been used as rat bait, the sap is poisonous and was used for arrow poison in Samoa, and leaf compounds are used as fish poison.[11] Most commercial products use refined or cold-pressed seed oil, which is the material the cosmetic research concerns.[1]

No studies found in humans for scars, acne or skin texture. A search of the biomedical literature for tamanu or Calophyllum inophyllum with patient or clinical-trial terms returned a 2021 review on atopic dermatitis and laboratory and animal work, but no human trial of the oil on skin.
Related laboratory and animal research is described above: cultured human skin cells,[3] a 21-rat wound-healing model,[7] an anti-scarring bigel study[8] and formulation studies.[10]

Tamanu oil is sold as a pure oil and as an ingredient in creams and serums labelled Calophyllum inophyllum seed oil.[2] Users describe applying it to scars, acne marks and dry skin by massaging it in, and its strong smell and thick texture are noted in product descriptions; no standardised regimen is described in the published research.[1][2]

card.summary: A Pacific nut oil promoted for scars and acne; lab cell data exist, human trials do not.
card.note: No clinical trial for scars or acne found.

quick.overview:
Tamanu oil comes from the nuts of a coastal tropical tree and has a long history in Pacific folk medicine.

It is sold for scars and acne. Lab studies on skin cells are encouraging in tone; human trials were not found.
quick.mechanism: In cell studies the oil raised skin-cell proliferation and collagen production; it also shows antioxidant activity.
quick.risks: Reported as low in toxicity at low concentrations; allergy data are limited.

chain: Oil is massaged onto skin or scars
Constituents are reported to act on inflammation, oxidation and skin-cell activity in lab studies
Skin looks smoother and marks look less prominent, as users describe
angle.text: Users apply tamanu oil to scars, acne marks and dry skin, expecting a smoother, more even surface. Lab and animal findings on wound healing and collagen production are cited as the rationale [3][7].
